passage: Counsellor's note. Mridul came to see me during the free period. He said his friend Sumit, usually the class joker, had been quiet for two weeks, yawning through lessons and missing the lunch table. Mridul had wondered whether to just leave it. Instead he sat next to Sumit on the bus and said, "How are you really?" Sumit answered that he was fine, then admitted he'd been sleeping badly because his family's shop had been struggling and everyone at home was tense. Mridul did not try to solve it. He listened, and then told me because he was a little worried. I thanked Mridul for both steps and arranged a quiet chat with Sumit for tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Mridul ask Sumit on the bus?
qa.a: He asked, 'How are you really?'

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: He felt a little worried, because Sumit's quietness, yawning and missing lunch had gone on for two weeks and Sumit's answer did not fully settle him.

qa.q: Why was telling the counsellor a sensible next step?
qa.a: Mridul could listen but couldn't fix a family problem, so passing on a real worry to a trusted adult was the right support for Sumit.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel about Mridul's question?
qa.a: He may feel relieved that someone noticed, though he first said he was fine, so he may also feel a little exposed.

grounding: A teen notices a friend who is quiet and tired, asks how he really is, and takes serious worry to a trusted adult.

passage: Thursday night. Sid barely laughed at any of my jokes today, and he didn't even fight me for the back seat on the bus. I didn't want to just guess, because I got it wrong last time when I thought he was angry with me. So at the bus stop I asked, "How are you really?" He blinked, then said he was tired and it was just the exams. I don't think that was the whole story, but he seemed glad I asked. He walked slowly home and didn't say goodbye the usual way. I'll ask him again on Saturday. If he still seems low then, I'm going to tell Mrs Nair, because I don't want to carry it alone. 🙂 - Manoj

qa.q: Where did Manoj ask Sid how he really was?
qa.a: Manoj asked at the bus stop.

qa.q: What does Manoj think about Sid's answer that it was just the exams?
qa.a: Manoj doesn't think it was the whole story, since Sid was quieter than usual and left without the usual goodbye, though he did seem glad to be asked.

qa.q: What will Manoj do if Sid still seems low on Saturday?
qa.a: Manoj plans to tell Mrs Nair, a trusted adult, so as not to carry the worry alone.

qa.q: How might Sid have felt when Manoj asked?
qa.a: He may have felt surprised and a bit relieved that someone noticed, even if he wasn't ready to say everything.

grounding: A teen diary shows reading a friend's quiet mood, asking gently, and planning to involve a trusted adult if worry continues.

passage:
In the small town of Champhai, the church youth choir practised every Thursday evening. Lalremsiami had noticed that Gargi, whose mother had come to teach at the school in June, had stopped humming along. She used to smile at everyone. Now she stood at the end of the row, eyes on her shoes, and left before tea.
Maybe she was just tired, Lalremsiami thought. Or maybe something was wrong.
On the third Thursday, she walked Gargi to the gate. "You seem quieter lately. How are you, really?"
Gargi was silent for a while. "I miss home. Lucknow. My grandparents. Everyone here knows each other since forever."
"That sounds lonely."
"It is a bit."
"Come for tea next time. My mother makes the best sticky rice. You can teach me a Lucknow song."
Gargi smiled properly for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: Where had Gargi's family come from?
qa.a: From Lucknow.

qa.q: What did Gargi's changed behaviour suggest to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: It suggested Gargi might be sad or lonely, though Lalremsiami knew it could also be tiredness, so she felt curious and concerned enough to ask.

qa.q: What made Lalremsiami's question effective?
qa.a: She asked privately and gently how Gargi really was, then responded with warmth and an invitation.

qa.q: How might Gargi have felt standing at the end of the choir row?
qa.a: She probably felt homesick and like an outsider in a group where everyone had known each other forever.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager noticing a friend who is quieter and asking gently instead of guessing.

passage:
In Stockholm, Lars had noticed for a month that Aiko had stopped making jokes in class. She came in tired, left early, and last week she'd given him her favourite comic series, "because I won't read them again."
On Friday, walking to the bus, he asked, "Aiko, how are you really?"
She shrugged. Then, very quietly: "I don't really see the point of anything anymore."
Lars felt his chest go cold. He didn't laugh or change the subject. "Thank you for telling me. I'm worried about you. Can we go to the school nurse together? Right now?"
She hesitated, then nodded.
They walked back in. The nurse listened carefully, thanked Aiko for coming, called the school counsellor to join them straight away, and phoned Aiko's mother. Lars waited outside until her mother arrived. Before he left, the counsellor said, "You did exactly the right thing."

qa.q: What had Aiko given Lars last week?
qa.a: Her favourite comic series.

qa.q: What was Lars feeling when Aiko said she didn't see the point?
qa.a: Lars felt frightened and deeply worried, his chest going cold, but stayed calm and caring.

qa.q: Which of Lars's choices were most important?
qa.a: Asking gently, taking her words seriously, and walking with her to the nurse immediately so trusted adults could act the same day.

qa.q: How did the nurse and counsellor respond, and why does it matter?
qa.a: They listened, thanked Aiko, brought in the counsellor straight away and called her mother, showing that serious worry is handled by caring adults at once.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager noticing a friend's lasting sadness, asking gently, and taking serious worry to trusted adults immediately.

passage: At the sports club, Anand had always been the loudest person on the badminton court, commentating on his own smashes. This week he hit quietly, missed easy shuttles and sat on the bench between games staring at his laces. Sharmila noticed he hadn't made a single joke in three sessions. She thought about guessing: a fight at home? Exams? Instead, at the water tap, she said, "You've been really quiet. How are you, really?" Anand shrugged, then said, "My grandfather's in hospital. I've been sleeping on the corridor bench to give Mum a break. I'm just tired." Sharmila didn't offer a pep talk. "That sounds so hard. Do you want me to tell Coach, so you're not in trouble for missing drills?" He hesitated, then nodded. Coach Mehra came over, sat on the bench beside him and said, "Train when you can. Rest is training too. Tell me what you need."

qa.q: Where has Anand been sleeping?
qa.a: Anand has been sleeping on the corridor bench at the hospital.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when Anand stopped joking?
qa.a: Sharmila felt curious and a bit worried, tempted to guess at a fight or exams, but chose to ask instead of deciding.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Sharmila asked a gentle 'How are you, really?' instead of guessing, listened without a pep talk, and with Anand's agreement brought in Coach, who offered flexibility.

qa.q: What was the week like for Anand?
qa.a: Anand was exhausted and worried about his grandfather, sleeping in the corridor, so he had no energy left for jokes or drills.

grounding: It shows a teenager noticing a peer being quiet and tired, asking gently rather than guessing, and involving a trusted adult.
